title: Government persuasion in numbers
heading: How far off is your gut?
intro: Eight real numbers about governments trying to change what we do: posters, packaging, defaults and advertising.
Every figure is real and sourced. Bet on how sure you are.

outro.heading: Governments have always tried to persuade.
paras: Posters, packaging, defaults and advertising budgets: some of these surprised the room more than others.
Where persuasion ends and manipulation begins is a line every society draws for itself.

questions.q: The 'Keep Calm and Carry On' poster was designed by Britain's Ministry of Information in 1939. What happened to it?
options: It was printed but almost never put up
It went up all over Britain
It was shown only in Scotland
It was banned as too gloomy
questions.explain: About 2.45 million copies were printed to be used in a crisis such as an invasion, but the poster was hardly ever displayed and most were pulped. A copy found in a bookshop in Alnwick in 2000 made it famous sixty years late.
questions.source: The National Archives; Imperial War Museums

questions.q: In 2020, which organisation was the biggest advertiser in the UK?
questions.explain: Its Covid-19 campaigns ('Stay home, protect the NHS, save lives') made the UK government the country's biggest advertiser in 2020, spending about £164m, ahead of Unilever, Sky and Procter & Gamble. Most of the money went on telling people what the rules were and why to follow them.
questions.source: Nielsen advertising spend data, reported by Campaign, January 2021

questions.q: Organ donation now works on an 'opt-out' basis across the UK: adults count as donors unless they say no. Which part of the UK made the switch first?
questions.explain: Wales switched in December 2015, followed by England (May 2020), Scotland (March 2021) and Northern Ireland (June 2023). Changing the default is one of the quietest ways a government can change behaviour.

questions.q: Which country was the first to require cigarettes to be sold in plain packs, with no logos or brand colours?
questions.explain: Australia's plain packaging rules took full effect on 1 December 2012, months after the tobacco industry lost a challenge in its High Court. The UK followed in 2016–17, and many countries have since copied it.
questions.source: Tobacco Tactics (University of Bath), Plain Packaging; High Court of Australia, August 2012

questions.q: What share of UK adults smoked cigarettes in 2025?
questions.explain: 9.8% of adults smoked in 2025, about 4.9 million people and the lowest share since the current series began in 2011 (20.2%). In the mid-1970s it was around 45%. Taxes, bans, warnings and campaigns all played a part.
questions.source: ONS, Adult smoking habits in the UK: 2025 (October 2026); General Household Survey, 1974

questions.q: Since 2012, UK employers must put workers into a workplace pension automatically; workers can opt out. What share of eligible employees now save into one?
questions.explain: Participation rose from 55% of eligible employees in 2012 to 90% in 2025, about 22.6 million people. Nobody was forced to save: the government changed the default, and most people simply did not opt out.
questions.source: DWP, Workplace pension participation and savings trends, 2009 to 2025 (July 2026)

questions.q: After a 1998 paper falsely linked the MMR vaccine to autism, how low did MMR coverage for two-year-olds in England fall at its worst, in 2003–04?
questions.explain: Coverage fell from about 92% in the mid-1990s to 79.9% in 2003–04, and measles came back. The paper was retracted in 2010 and its lead author struck off the medical register.
questions.source: NHS Immunisation Statistics (COVER), 2003–04; The Lancet, retraction, 2010

questions.q: Which phrase did Collins Dictionary choose as its Word of the Year in 2017, after its use rose by 365%?
questions.explain: Collins chose 'fake news', defined as false, often sensational information spread under the guise of news reporting. 'Post-truth' was Oxford's word of the year in 2016; 'infodemic' and 'deepfake' came into wide use later.
questions.source: Collins Dictionary, Word of the Year 2017
